text:
The fifth came up the block the way ordinary people come up blocks. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't clock her until she was already inside the loose triangle the three of them made — and that bothered him more than if she'd dropped out of a window. His piece was the perimeter; his whole job on this crew was that nobody crossed a threshold he was watching without him watching them do it, and she'd just walked through his sightline like it was open air. So the first thing he did, before the coat and the face and the rest of it, was make himself read her — angle of approach, hands, the beat of her stride — the way you take apart a thing that beat you, so it doesn't beat you twice. She was medium. Medium height, a coat the color of a coat, hair pulled back the way you pull it back when you've stopped thinking about it. The kind of face a room rounds down to nothing, that a camera forgets before the timestamp finishes writing. You could ride an elevator with her and swear a week later you'd ridden up alone.

"<entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity>," she said, for the channel. The codename and the whole introduction, three years of freighter holds and cold noodles folded flat behind it. She said it the way you give a barista a name you don't expect to hear called back.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read her anyway, the way he always did. Quiet, polite, forgettable on purpose. That was a skill, not an accident, and a skill that took that much work to look like nothing was usually pointed at something. Three years, and he still didn't know exactly what she did. The brief hadn't said. On a clean crew the brief never told you more than your own piece — Shroud knew the building, Stash knew the gear, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew his piece was to stand between everyone else and whatever came through a door. If the brief kept <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity>'s piece from him, that meant hers was the one the client cared about. And the client had a longer reach than the name that had handed the job down, which was as far up the chain as <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was ever meant to see.

"You're the muscle," she said to him, deadpan, for the crew. Not a question. Then she tilted her head, the way she had the first time, in a freighter hold three years ago, when she'd already decided to like the answer. "What do I call you?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> opened his mouth. He got one syllable out — maybe less, the K of his name — and Shroud's voice came flat into the channel. *No real names.*

He closed his mouth. He looked around. The corner. The rain. The shuttered pharmacy with Stash's weight still denting the doorway. And down by the base of the step, carried there from somewhere else by the gutter, a glass soda bottle with a faded orange label.

"Soda Pop," he said.

<entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> snorted. A real snort, unguarded — the first thing she'd done tonight that wasn't careful, and it did to her plain face what it had done the first time.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> picked up the bottle and threw it against the pharmacy wall. The glass went everywhere, sharp and sudden, the small violence of it heavier than the sound it made — not a crash, a clean and specific sound, a glass sound.

"Broken Glass," he said.

She made the same sound again, working now to keep it in. She looked at the pieces on the wet concrete. She looked at him. Three years of the same bit, and it still landed.

"That's not a tactical skill," she said.

"No."

"That's why it works." She looked at him one beat longer — not a read now, just confirming he was there. "I'm just going to call you K." The way she always did. The shorter version, the one that meant something different when she said it like a question.

He went back to watching the street, and didn't look too hard at why it mattered that she'd kept the K.

The transmission completed. <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> said, "Clean." One word. The job's word for done.

The thing came up the ramp before the echo died — not running, just arriving. Four arms. Three of them were shotguns, the barrels socketed straight into the wrist housings, where a normal man's hands would be. This one had spent real money to stop being a normal man. The fourth arm carried something belt-fed, a chain running back through the shoulder housing.

It didn't announce itself. It didn't give her a chance.

It had the angle on her before <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was moving. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was moving before the decision reached him. He was already moving when it no longer mattered.

The first round came up through <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity>'s ribs and out through her shoulder blade. The sound was wrong — not the crack of a rifle but a subsonic thump, the round so heavy and slow it didn't cut the air, just punched through it. <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> went down. She went down the way you go down when you're still trying to understand what happened, her knees folding before her hands had time to catch her.

title: Three Barrels
text:
The first shotgun spoke, and the loading dock answered in dust. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> wasn't where the dust was. He'd read the lead arm a quarter-second before the wrist committed — the way the shoulder loaded, the way a man with three barrels still aims with his eyes — and he'd gone low and wide, off the line, behind the concrete pillar that would hold up against buckshot. A freelancer's cover wouldn't have. The blast took a bite out of the bay door behind where he'd been, and the noise was a flat hand against both ears.

Subsonic. Heavy. The kind of load that didn't crack the air so much as remove whatever it touched.

The read was simple. <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> had four rounds left in <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">the cylinder</entity>. <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity>'s belt-fed arm held more than that, and nobody wins a trade against a wall of fire. So <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> kept <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> and <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> in his hands, <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> a line of matte black between him and the guns. The blade was an argument for close distance. The only way through a wall of fire was to be past it before it knew you'd moved.

One of <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity>'s grenades had bounced wrong in the clearing pattern. It came to rest six feet from the column, its arming light cycling toward the end of its count.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> picked it up.

The NeoCortex had no governor. That was the thing killing him, and it was the only reason the next three seconds were possible. He connected to the detonator port through his neuretics and found the lock on the countdown — a rolling cipher, built to make disarming it in the field impossible. He broke it. Not with finesse. With raw processing power, the way you use a sledgehammer when you can't find the key, running through the cipher faster than the hardware was ever rated to go. The heat came up behind his eyes like a filament burning at both ends, and under it, small and unhurried, the thought he didn't let finish: *one more push like that and something in here stops coming back.* He'd had that thought before. He kept doing the push anyway, because being right about the cipher mattered more, right now, than the arithmetic of what it cost him — and some nights that ordering scared him worse than <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity> did.

He stopped the countdown with eight seconds left. He set the grenade near the mouth of the ramp exit and left it there.

Then he used the dock. The bay was a stack of crates, a lift platform, and a steel stairwell climbing to the loading office, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> made <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity> spend his fire on plywood. He didn't run from the guns. He ran the room around them, so every shot landed where he'd just been, and every half-second the three arms took to cycle their breeches put him one step closer. <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity> was fast — servo-driven, no lag between decision and movement — but he was also heavy, and heavy had to commit. Each repositioning cost him a fraction longer than it should have, the mass of the integrated systems dragging against the speed of the pivot, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> lived in those fractions. The torso turned to follow him on a ring that moved independent of the legs. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt the lead arm track him through a stack of cartons and threw himself off the line a breath before the boards turned to air.

"Pillar's chewed," Shroud said, fast, in his ear. She'd gotten clear but still had eyes on the structure from outside, her thermal scope reading through the dock's steel skin. "You can't trade. He's got a belt-feed on the left arm, he doesn't run dry —"

"I know what he doesn't do," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, and went up the stairwell.

It was the wrong direction. That was the point. A man fighting three shotguns runs for the exit. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> ran for the high steel, because a stair is a corridor, and a corridor turned three barrels into one.

The stair held for four steps. On the fifth, <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity> put a round through the riser under <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s back foot, and the whole flight dropped out from under him at once — steel tearing off its bolts with a shriek that had no business coming out of something that heavy, the landing rushing up gray and fast, no time left to pick where he fell.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hit the landing hard enough that his vision went white at the edges.

The impact took him across the ribs—the bad side, the one <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had stitched—and something that had been holding decided it was done holding. Pain bloomed white-hot and specific, a seam opening under the bandage line, and his breath came back in a shape that wasn't quite a breath. He lay there for the half-second it took his body to remember how to move, and in that half-second the stairwell's shriek stopped, and the dock went quiet except for the sound of <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity>'s legs dragging him forward.

The grenade ticked.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> rolled onto his front and got his hands under him. The rib screamed. He ignored it the way you ignore a siren when you're trying to hear something else—acknowledged it, filed it, kept moving. The stairwell had come down in a heap of steel and bolt-work, three flights' worth of corridor suddenly converted into a maze of sharp edges and twisted railings. It was also cover. It was also between him and the ramp exit where the grenade was counting down.

He could see <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity>'s shape through the tangle—the torso a clean silhouette against the dock's flood-lights, the three arms cycling through their reloads with the methodical patience of something that didn't need to breathe hard. The left arm was still feeding. The middle arm was up. The right arm was tracking for the sound.

The grenade had maybe eight seconds left.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moved through the wreckage like it was water, using the fallen steel as a ladder and a shield both, keeping his profile small and his movement economical. His left shoulder was still half-numb from the contact tool discharge—the nerve coming back in patches, pins-and-needles sensation mixing with the phantom memory of paralysis—but he had enough of his hand to grip. Enough of his arm to drive.

<entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity>'s head rotated toward the noise of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> moving.

The torso followed a half-second behind, the ring-mount catching up to the targeting vector, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was already off the line, using the stairwell's twisted guardrail as a vaulting point to shift left and down into a pocket of shadow between two fallen sections. A burst from the right arm chewed through the space he'd just occupied, buckshot ricocheting off steel with a sound like breaking glass.

The grenade had five seconds.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> came up from the shadow and moved toward the loading office door—not the exit, not yet, but the high ground that overlooked the dock. The stairwell had been the narrow corridor he'd needed. The office was the next layer: a place where three barrels became a liability instead of a weapon.

<entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity> saw the movement and committed to a burst from the middle arm, leading <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s trajectory with the cold precision of something that had already calculated exactly where he'd be. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> felt the rounds pass close enough to register the heat bloom, and he didn't correct his line or slow down. Instead he accelerated into it, because the only winning move against predictive fire was to be faster than the prediction's margin of error. The next burst would correct. The burst after that would correct again. But there was always a lag—a half-second where the targeting system had to update—and in that half-second <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hit the office door frame and went through sideways, rolling across the threshold into darkness.

The grenade detonated.

The sound was enormous and clean, a sharp crack that didn't scatter the way buckshot did. The blast pressure came through the office window and rattled the frame, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> heard <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity> hit something solid—not the grenade's full force, but the edge of it, enough to disrupt whatever calculus had been keeping him mobile. A sound like machinery failing. A sound like something heavy landing badly.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stayed in the darkness for two full breaths, waiting for his eyes to adjust, waiting for the NeoCortex's thermal overlay to resolve the space. The office was small—a desk, a chair, filing cabinets, and a window that looked down on the dock. His vision came back in layers: first the shapes, then the heat signatures, then the detail. Empty except for him.

He moved to the window.

<entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity> was on his back in the center of the dock, and his left arm—the belt-fed arm, the one that didn't run dry—was hanging limp at the socket. The right-front leg wasn't moving. The torso's rotation ring was stuck mid-turn, frozen at an angle that shouldn't have been possible for something with a hinge.

One arm still tracked. The middle arm, the one that had been cycling for the last exchange. It moved with mechanical slowness, searching for a target that was no longer in the sight line, and then it went still.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> watched him for a full ten seconds. <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity>'s single good arm—the left rear—started to move. Not toward <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. Away. Down the ramp, pulling what was left of his chassis toward the street beyond, toward the city beyond that.

*You are not protected. You are necessary.*

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't move. He watched <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity> crawl into the darkness of the ramp, watched the sound of him fade into the ambient noise of the dock, watched the moment <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity> stopped being a threat and started being something else—something broken and mobile and gone.

Then he turned away from the window and looked at the filing cabinet in the corner.

The office was small enough that he could see everything in it. That was the thing about high ground. You could see what you were standing on top of. And what <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was standing on top of was a room full of records, and a door that led back down to the dock, and a corpse still wearing a stall-vendor's coat, waiting for him to come back down and acknowledge what it meant that she was gone.

He didn't move toward the door yet.

Instead he sat down on the edge of the desk—carefully, favoring the right side, not trusting the rib to hold his full weight—and he let himself feel the weight of what had just happened. The calculations that had seemed so simple in the moment—the cipher, the grenade, the stairwell as a corridor—those calculations had a cost that didn't announce itself in real-time. The cost was in his hands shaking now that they didn't have anything to do. The cost was in his breath still not quite finding its rhythm. The cost was in knowing that he'd made <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity>'s choice for him, that he'd positioned the grenade and left it there, that he'd forced the equation that had ended with <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity> crawling away rather than staying.

*The blade does not lie. Only the hand holding it.*

He'd held <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>. He'd held it all the way through.

He pressed both palms flat on the desk. The tremor continued anyway.

The NeoCortex ran a thermal diagnostic he could feel like a second heartbeat behind his eyes—feedback loops cycling, checking for cascade failure, finding nothing yet but promising to find it soon. His left arm hung at an angle that suggested the joint had opinions about its current load-bearing status. The rib screamed when he breathed. The shoulder was a study in wet heat, the kind that didn't stop bleeding just because the round had passed through.

<entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity> was gone. Not dead. Gone. The distinction mattered less than it should have.

*You forced that outcome.*

The thought arrived unannounced, the way unwanted thoughts did when the adrenaline was draining and the body was still counting casualties. What he'd held <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> *through* was a man who'd been following orders from someone <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> still hadn't identified, doing work <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> still didn't understand, in a building <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had been directed to by a contract that claimed to come from nowhere.

The filing cabinet was locked, but the lock was mechanical and old, the kind that had been installed before anyone thought to upgrade to electronic. He found a letter opener on the desk—actual steel, actual weight—and worked it into the gap. The first drawer came open with a sound like something small dying.

Inside: shipping manifests. Way bills. Dock assignments dated back seven years. Nothing that moved. Nothing that explained the office, the ambush, or why the entity had routed a contract to a carousel assessment that led here instead of to the carousel.

The second drawer held something else.

A relay terminal, dead and dark, no bigger than his palm. The kind that took input, sent output, talked to something bigger—the kind that sat in a field office and routed contracts back to a central system. He turned it over. No serial number visible; the back panel was sealed with a polymer that would take a cutting tool to breach. Then he found the stencil on the casing, and his stomach dropped: *<entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">CONTINUITY OFFICE</entity> - RESTRICTED*.

He didn't touch it further. He photographed it with the NeoCortex's passive optics—three angles, the screen dormant, the cable still connected to the wall jack—held each shot steady long enough for the lens to lock focus, logged what serial architecture he could read off the housing, and moved to the third drawer.

This one was unlocked. Inside: a single folder, paper, handwritten labels. The kind of record that didn't exist in any system because the system wasn't supposed to know about it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> opened it.

The first page was a photograph. Not recent. Not from the facility. From somewhere else, somewhere he didn't remember being photographed—taken from an angle that suggested surveillance rather than booking. His face was younger, angrier, looking at something off-camera with an expression he didn't remember wearing, and the image quality was low enough to suggest it had been extracted from surveillance footage.

Behind it, an operations sheet, most of it gone under a censor's marker — hand-drawn strokes, not a printer's redaction. What survived: a section header, *ASSET DISPOSITION*, with everything underneath it removed. A stamped line at the bottom, three words. SUBJECT: STILL ACTIVE.

He was looking at his own file, or what someone had decided he was allowed to see of it.

*You are necessary.*

He understood, in that moment, what necessary meant, even with most of the page blacked out. It didn't mean valued. It didn't mean protected. It meant that someone, somewhere, was still tracking him closely enough to keep a file open and current—to catalogue him like a piece of equipment and file him on a <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">Continuity Office</entity> header. It meant every contract, every job, every moment of this eleven-year thread had been part of a shape he could feel now without being able to read it — a ledger with his photograph on it and his name inked out along with everything else.

The folder hit the floor.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> turned toward the door—the one that led back down to the dock, back to the body of the woman who had called him "K" and meant it as a kindness, back to the equation that had ended with her dead and him alive and the weight of it settling into his shoulders like a second spine.

He had a problem.

The entity had sent him here to assess a carousel. Instead he'd found a redacted file with his own photograph in it and proof that someone besides the entity was watching him closely enough to keep it current. He'd forced <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity> into a choice that ended with the machine crawling away broken. He'd left <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> on the dock in a coat that probably cost more than she'd made in a month.

And somewhere in the city, a relay terminal was waiting to report that his evaluation was complete.

His hands had stopped shaking.

The rib still screamed. The shoulder still bled. The left arm still hung at an angle that suggested the joint had a grievance. But the hands were steady again, and the mind behind them had moved past the moment of revelation into something colder and more useful.

He picked up the folder.

He didn't look at the photograph again. He simply tucked the file into his jacket, against his ribs where the stitches were still fresh, next to the proof he was supposed to deliver at midnight. A few ounces of paper. No encryption, no security protocol beyond a marker and a prayer that nobody would look too close—and it felt heavier than that, heavier than the terminal would have. He walked back toward the door.

<entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> was waiting. The dock was waiting. And somewhere in the city, an entity that had spent eleven years building him toward this moment was filing the details under *FIRSTS* and deciding what necessary meant next.

He descended the ramp into the dark.

title: Who Vouches for You
text:
<entity repo="character" guid="fe6ab919-9f3c-450b-aaf5-f24f84896521">Stash</entity> had pulled the van back from the bay and stood in the gap between the rear bumper and the dock's concrete wall. They'd laid their coat over her. The shape under it was small and final, and the hem of the coat was dark with something that wouldn't wash out. Their hands were still at the hem where they'd smoothed it down — the hands of someone who'd run out of work to do and hadn't moved them yet.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stopped. He put <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> away.

"She was already —" <entity repo="character" guid="fe6ab919-9f3c-450b-aaf5-f24f84896521">Stash</entity> started.

"I know," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019eafb5-3337-764f-8fb0-75dc82170edf">Ledger</entity> stood on the far side of the van, looking at nothing in particular. That was the look <entity repo="character" guid="019eafb5-3337-764f-8fb0-75dc82170edf">Ledger</entity> had when he was paying the most attention. He'd been at his position. The vehicle had come from below. He would put it in the report, and the report wouldn't make it make sense, because there was no sense to make.

"We need to move," <entity repo="character" guid="fe6ab919-9f3c-450b-aaf5-f24f84896521">Stash</entity> said. "Shroud's already clear."

"I know," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said again. The dock smelled like old concrete and cold off Lake Michigan and the hydraulic fluid still bleeding out of the arm three stories down. He owed her one beat, unhurried.

Then he picked her up, coat and all, the way <entity repo="character" guid="fe6ab919-9f3c-450b-aaf5-f24f84896521">Stash</entity> had laid it, and set her in the back of the van himself. <entity repo="character" guid="fe6ab919-9f3c-450b-aaf5-f24f84896521">Stash</entity>'s van. Their work vehicle, the one they drove for the Vultures jobs, the one that had carried this kind of weight before.

The body was evidence. That was true. A Read's mind didn't go dark at death the way a normal person's did — not right away, not with the right equipment. Put the brain in a tank of conducting fluid, run electrodes through the right structures, and what she knew was still in there: the client's name, the data she'd pulled, the job, the faces on the team. Someone with the money and the reason could pull the last hours out of a dead psionic's head and use them to kill every person in this van. That was true too.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew both true things.

He carried her anyway. You did not leave a comrade behind.

He got in.

The van doors closed on darkness and the smell of copper.

Stash took the wheel without asking where. There was only one direction that made sense: away from the dock, away from the structure's shadow, toward the gray-zone perimeter where the Vultures had standing contracts to move bodies without questions. The engine turned over. The hydraulic suspension compressed under the load.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat on the bench seat beside the body, his left arm still hanging at the wrong angle, his right hand pressed against the rib wound because the bandage <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had stitched had finally given up pretending it was doing any work. The folder in his jacket was a small hard weight against his sternum. Above that: a file he still couldn't read past its own redactions. Below that: the midnight proof that was supposed to buy him something he couldn't name anymore.

The van's radio crackled. Ledger's voice came through: *"Clear north of Halsted. Two checkpoints dark. Route holds."*

Stash didn't acknowledge. Just drove. The city moved past the reinforced windows in grayscale — the loading platforms giving way to warehouse facades, the facades giving way to the vertical sprawl of the industrial tier. Every block they crossed was a block that wouldn't ask questions. Every checkpoint they cleared was a checkpoint that wouldn't file a report.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the shape under the coat.

<entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> had worked with him for three years. No first name ever given. No story ever told. She'd been in the cargo hold of a freighter when he'd met her, sorting through a data-theft job with the kind of precision that suggested she'd done this exact work a thousand times before. He'd given himself the handle *Broken Glass* in the first five minutes — a bottle against a freighter wall, the night Shroud said no real names — and she'd decided it was funny. Then she'd reduced it to *K* because the shorter version meant something different when you said it like a question mark instead of a statement.

*Did you know?* the shorter version asked. *Do you understand what this costs?*

He didn't answer the dead woman.

The van took a hard left onto a service corridor that didn't appear on any map Stash would admit to knowing. The suspension bottomed out on broken concrete. Somewhere in the back, equipment shifted — the tools of the Vultures trade: the fluid tanks, the preservation cases, the refrigeration units that made this particular kind of transport possible. The van smelled like a tomb on wheels.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s asking for status," Ledger said over the radio. "She's asking if you're moving or if you're staying."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s jaw tightened. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was at the yard, waiting for a signal that would tell her whether to stand down or proceed with the next phase of the operation. Whether to assume <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was operational or whether to assume the dock had taken him the way it had taken <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity>.

"Tell her I'm moving," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"She's asking if you're intact."

The question had weight. *Intact* didn't mean alive. It meant functional. It meant the hardware was holding. It meant the mind behind the hardware was still making decisions instead of executing subroutines. It meant the person in the van was still a person and not a program running its final sequence.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked down at his hands. They were steady. They were his. The shaking had stopped somewhere between the office and the dock, somewhere in the moment when he'd accepted that the file in his jacket was proof of something he'd already suspected: that the last eleven years had been a syllabus, and he was the only student who'd made it to the final exam.

"Tell her intact is relative," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Tell her we're moving to the pickup point. Tell her I'll know the answer to the rest of it by midnight."

Stash navigated the service corridor without speaking. That was Stash's way — the work came before the conversation, and the conversation came after the work was done. The van emerged onto a wider stretch of industrial tier, the kind of place where the city had stopped bothering to maintain the fiction of pedestrian infrastructure. Just loading docks and service ramps and the industrial haze that hung perpetually between the warehouses like a held breath.

"Ledger's saying Shroud cleared the eastern checkpoint clean," Stash said finally. "No tags. No followers. We're moving through known territory."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> nodded. That was important. It meant the operation hadn't been burned, which meant the entity's intelligence was still accurate, which meant the midnight delivery was still possible. It also meant that <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity>'s handlers — whoever had sent the quadrupedal killing machine into the dock with three functional arms and orders to clean the job — hadn't yet moved to intercept the exfil.

Yet.

"How much time do we have?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"Until what?"

"Until the Port Authority sweep reaches this sector."

Stash's hands tightened on the wheel. "Hour and a half. Maybe two if we're lucky and they hit the south dock first."

An hour and a half to move the body. An hour and a half to reach a Vultures drop point where <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> would become a statistical correction in a ledger that no one official would ever read. An hour and a half before the zone authority's automated sweeps started cataloging bodies and filing incident reports that would eventually cross someone's desk with the weight of a decision.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s left arm had started to regain sensation. Not movement yet — the contact discharge had fried the nerve pathway and it would take hours for his neuretics to rebuild the connection — but sensation. A dull electric ache that ran from collarbone to fingertip, the kind of pain that reminded you that you were still intact enough to feel.

He flexed his fingers. Three of them responded. Two stayed locked.

"Tell <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> we're delayed," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Tell her the dock was compromised and we're taking the long route. Tell her to hold position and wait for confirmation."

"She's not going to like that."

"She doesn't have to."

The van moved through the city like a burial at speed. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat with the body and the folder and the eleven-year-old question that still had no answer: *Who am I?* Not <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. Not Ellen. Not <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Corbin</entity>. Whoever that was, the file wasn't telling — someone had made sure of that before it ever reached him.

The entity had sent him to assess a carousel. Instead it had sent him to find the grave of his own history.

*You are necessary.*

He understood now. Necessary wasn't a compliment. It was a sentence. It meant that someone had calculated the trajectory and found it useful. It meant that every choice he'd made for eleven years had been a choice the entity had already seen coming. It meant that the moment he'd opened that folder, he'd stopped being a person making decisions and had started being a probability cascade executing the only sequence that would produce the outcome someone else had already designed.

Except.

Except he'd let <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">War</entity> <entity repo="character" guid="1e31f7e6-a5d6-4bd1-94b8-8d33dfd7f5d1">Dog</entity> go.

That wasn't in any sequence. That wasn't in any calculation. The entity had positioned him at the dock to neutralize a threat, and instead he'd pushed the machine toward the edge and watched it choose its own exit. He'd made a choice that wasn't on the board.

It was small. It was probably meaningless. But it was his.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> picked up the folder again. This time he opened it. He looked at the photograph of a face that was supposed to be his and didn't feel like it. He let the not-knowing sit in his chest like a second wound.

Then he folded the photograph in half and put it back.

"Stash," he said.

"Yeah?"

"After the drop. After we clear the Vultures point. I need you to take me somewhere."

"Where?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the body under the coat. <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> had asked him once, over cold noodles in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the Gray Zone</entity>, whether he believed in debt. Whether he thought that owing someone something was a real thing or just a story people told themselves to make the unbearable feel like it had a shape.

He'd told her it was real. He'd told her that debt was the only honest thing in a city built on lies.

She'd laughed. She'd said: *Then you're going to carry a lot of weight before this is over, K.*

She'd been right.

"I need you to take me to <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "I need to tell her that <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity>'s dead, and I need to do it before she hears it from someone else."

Stash didn't answer for a long moment. The van moved through the industrial sector, toward the drop point, toward the moment when they'd hand the body over to the Vultures and become statistical ghosts in a system that didn't count the dead the way the living counted them.

"That's not the midnight route," Stash said finally.

"No," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> agreed. "It's not."

"It's going to cost you time."

"I know."

Stash took the next turn toward the sector boundary, where the Vultures had a depot that didn't appear on any map. "Then we do it your way. We drop <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity>, we move to Chen's, and then we figure out how you make the midnight run from the other side of the city."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> nodded. It was the right choice. It was also the expensive one.

The van's radio stayed silent. Ledger was holding position. Shroud was clear. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was waiting at the yard for confirmation that never came. And somewhere in the city's electrical grid, a relay terminal was filing reports in a format only the entity could read.

The folder against his sternum felt heavier with every block.

By the time they reached the Vultures depot — a reinforced loading bay built into the basement of a condemned arcology tower — the hour had compressed to forty-five minutes. The sweeps would be moving north soon. The body would be processed, tagged, filed, and disappeared into the cold-chain infrastructure that made <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the Gray Zone</entity>'s mortality rate mathematically invisible.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> carried <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity>'s body inside. He didn't look at her face. He didn't say anything. <entity repo="faction" guid="0260c60e-7a18-b1e4-d5f6-a708b9c0d1e2">The Vultures</entity> knew the protocol. They took the coat, the personal effects, the weight. The rest was procedure — the tanks waiting in the dark, the preservation cases already open, the fee already deducted from a balance no bank held. You arrived in the window. You left the package. You didn't ask what happened to the package after.

When he came back out, Stash was waiting with the engine running.

"<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

Stash pulled into traffic without acknowledging. They moved through <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a94e-7740-8aa9-4b82bbd9a223">the Gray Zone</entity> in the direction of the noodle counter, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat in the passenger seat with his hand on his ribs and the folder in his jacket and the knowledge that he'd just bought himself a detour that might cost him the midnight delivery.

But there were some debts that couldn't wait.

The city moved past the windows in grayscale. Somewhere above them, the float layer hummed with the weight of money and distance. Somewhere below, the Vultures were already forgetting <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity>'s name. And somewhere in the electrical substrate, the entity was recalculating the new sequence, adjusting for the one choice <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had made that wasn't on the board.

The entity had spent eleven years building him.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had just spent forty-five minutes proving it wasn't finished yet.

At the second light north, the channel chirped once.

A fresh posting. Pushed wide to every freelancer band in the van's radius — not targeted, not narrow, the kind of push the relay gave anything it flagged as time-sensitive. The full broadcast tone, not the soft ping that meant routine work. The sound that pulled every operator with an active feed out of whatever they were doing and made them look. Clean scope. Listed retainer. A client field that resolved to a shell, and the shell to nothing.

Stash went quiet in the way of someone who has just run a number and doesn't like where it lands. They kept their eyes on the road. They didn't check the mirror.

Ledger read the posting the way you read a threat — fast, for the shape of it, not the details. Extraction and transport. Φ8,000 base plus contingency. A relay-only contact, encrypted, no voice, no face. Then he looked at the back of the van. Then he read it again.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat with the glass through the lining of his coat pocket and didn't open the posting. He could feel it sitting in the buffer anyway, the relay's standard delivery for anyone running Tier 3 and above — a pressure behind the left eye, waiting to be acknowledged. He didn't acknowledge it.

An hour since the dock. The relay didn't know that. Or it didn't care. Or it had known before they even left, and the posting had been ready, and the second light north was the exact second light north?

He watched the rain on the windshield and didn't think about it.

He would open it in the morning. He would take the job. He had a funeral to price.

The night the dock job ended, her field kit was smaller than usual. That meant she'd done the triage before she knocked — worked out what he'd need and packed for exactly that. Not the full kit. The one calibrated for a night when a man shows up carrying something he has to set down before he'll let anyone near the wounds.

"Sit," she said.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sat. A year ago he'd have argued — something about field medicine and letting someone with suturing and wound treatment keep her independence. The argument didn't come. He opened his jacket without being asked.

She didn't say anything about that.

There was one thing he wanted from tonight, and it wasn't the medicine. He wanted to get through it without saying <entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity>'s name aloud again — to let her patch the body and leave the rest sealed, to sit still long enough that the silence held instead of cracking. That was the whole of it. Stay quiet. Stay closed. Let her work and let the name stay where he'd set it down in the van.

She worked the damage in order. The cut above his ear, from the corner of a rack casing — she cleaned it and closed it with the med-sealant, the professional grade, the kind that came in small bottles from clinics that didn't ask for ID, that cost Φ and held for a week before it started to break down. The deep bruise across his ribs, which she found through the shirt before she saw it. His right palm, which had taken a rail edge in a way that wouldn't heal in under a week. She read each one the way she read a fault code — timestamp, vector, what the hardware was telling her — and dressed it with the flat economy of someone who'd been thinking about this since she heard how the job ended.

<entity repo="character" guid="05fbd9d0-c6d5-4731-8e48-f1a4c59e8783">Sift</entity> was dead. Two truths sat in that — the operational one and the human one. He'd said them both in the van, in the order they had to come. Then he'd done the only thing left, which was nothing.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> ran the sealant along the palm in one smooth line. It hardened fast, pulling the edges together with a tight, burning pressure. She set the dressing over it and smoothed it flat with two fingers. She didn't ask.

That was the thing. The not asking.

He sat in the chair with the lamp going and the rain outside and the coupling splice still on the table from whenever she'd left it. The music in the corner — something with teeth, something that had been playing when he came in — kept its rhythm through the work. She moved through the damage and offered him nothing but the medicine. It was the most useful thing anyone had done for him in a week. He didn't say so. She didn't need him to.

"Done," she said.

"Done," he said.

She made tea after that. He didn't ask for it and didn't turn it down. It just arrived — loose leaf in a paper sachet, the kind that came from somewhere <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> didn't advertise. Not the street blend. The good one.

She sat across from him at the workbench with her own cup and set a small oval pill on the table between them. He knew the kind. You took it after a bad job, when your nervous system kept running the scenario on a loop and sleep wasn't coming for hours. She snapped it in half with her thumbnail — neat, no drama — and slid one half toward him.

He picked it up. He wanted one thing out of the next hour: to sit here long enough that the docks stopped playing behind his eyes, and to not screw that up by talking about them.

She put the other half on her tongue, chased it with tea, and looked out at the rain.

He did the same. Tea and rain. The coupling splice still waiting on the table. The lamp buzzing very quietly overhead. The city outside not asking anything of anyone. They sat while the edge came off. Somewhere in there it had become late — he'd lost the evening down at the docks.

"I made a self-adhesive gasket seal that holds at fifteen atmospheres," she said at one point. "I want you to know that's more impressive than it sounds."

"I know it is," he said.

"I just like saying it," she said.

They sat until the light changed. Below, the noodle cart made its last announcement of the night. <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> had been calling that sound criminal since the cart showed up three years ago. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had privately decided it was comforting. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> fell asleep sitting up at some point, chin on her fist, the empty cup still in her other hand.

He didn't move. The hour was fine.
